subject: economics
topicDisplay: Theme 2 The UK Economy Performance And Policies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The trade (business) cycle describes:
options: Short-term fluctuations of actual output around the trend rate of growth
The long-run upward trend of potential output
The relationship between inflation and unemployment
The balance between exports and imports over time
questions.explain: The trade cycle is the pattern of booms, slowdowns, recessions and recoveries of actual GDP around its long-run trend.

questions.q: The monetary transmission mechanism describes how:
options: Productivity growth raises potential output
A change in interest rates affects AD through channels such as borrowing, saving, asset prices and the exchange rate
Banks create money through lending
Tax changes feed through to government revenue
questions.explain: The transmission mechanism is the process by which a change in the policy rate influences spending and inflation via borrowing costs, asset prices, confidence and the exchange rate.

questions.q: The distinction between a budget (fiscal) deficit and the national debt is that:
options: The deficit only includes interest payments
They are two names for the same thing
The deficit is an annual flow; the national debt is the accumulated stock of borrowing
The national debt is annual; the deficit is the total stock
questions.explain: A fiscal deficit is the annual excess of spending over revenue (a flow); the national debt is the total stock of accumulated government borrowing.

questions.q: The accelerator theory states that investment depends on:
options: The absolute level of national income
The rate of change of national income/output
The level of government spending
The rate of interest only
questions.explain: The accelerator relates investment to the rate of change of output, so rising demand induces proportionally larger investment.

questions.q: Frictional unemployment refers to people who are:
options: Out of work because of the time of year
Unemployed because of a fall in aggregate demand
Temporarily between jobs while searching for new work
Unemployed because their skills are obsolete
questions.explain: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment as workers move between jobs and search for suitable vacancies.

questions.q: Fiscal policy is generally regarded as effective at boosting AD during a deep recession because:
options: Interest rates always rise sharply
Crowding out is severe when resources are scarce
With spare capacity, government spending can raise output and employment with a strong multiplier and little crowding out
It has no impact on the multiplier
questions.explain: In a recession with idle resources, the multiplier is larger and crowding out is minimal, so fiscal stimulus can effectively raise output.

questions.q: Which of the following would cause the SRAS curve to shift to the left?
options: A fall in raw material costs
Greater spare capacity in the economy
A rise in business taxes such as VAT or employment taxes
An increase in the productivity of labour
questions.explain: Higher costs of production, such as increased indirect or employment taxes, raise firms' costs and shift SRAS to the left.

questions.q: A trade-off of using contractionary policy to reduce inflation is that it may:
options: Increase economic growth
Improve all macroeconomic objectives simultaneously
Cause higher unemployment and slower growth in the short run
Reduce the national debt instantly
questions.explain: Reducing AD to control inflation tends to lower output and raise unemployment in the short run, illustrating a policy conflict.

questions.q: A cyclical budget deficit differs from a structural deficit in that a cyclical deficit:
options: Is the same as the national debt
Is unaffected by the level of output
Persists even at full employment
Arises automatically because of the economic cycle and falls as the economy recovers
questions.explain: A cyclical deficit results from the downturn (lower tax revenue, higher benefits) and shrinks in recovery, unlike a structural deficit which remains at full employment.

questions.q: One supply-side benefit claimed for reducing the power of trade unions is that it may:
options: Improve labour market flexibility and reduce structural unemployment
Raise the natural rate of unemployment
Increase cost-push inflation
Reduce the size of the workforce
questions.explain: Reducing union power is argued to increase wage flexibility and labour mobility, lowering frictional and structural unemployment.

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy involves:
options: Cutting government spending to reduce the deficit
Higher interest rates set by the central bank
The central bank selling government bonds
Increased government spending and/or lower taxation
questions.explain: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government spending and/or cuts taxes to boost aggregate demand.

questions.q: Structural unemployment is caused primarily by:
options: Seasonal variation in demand for labour
Workers being temporarily between jobs
A general fall in aggregate demand in a recession
A mismatch between workers' skills and the skills employers require
questions.explain: Structural unemployment arises from a mismatch of skills (or location) as the structure of the economy changes, leaving workers' skills no longer in demand.

questions.q: A criticism of using interest rate cuts to stimulate the economy is that they:
options: Can be a 'blunt instrument' affecting all sectors and regions unequally and operate with time lags
Only affect government spending
Always cause an immediate rise in output
Have no effect on the exchange rate
questions.explain: Interest rate changes are a blunt, economy-wide tool with variable lags and uneven regional/sectoral effects, limiting precise control.

questions.q: Aggregate demand in an open economy is correctly expressed as:
options: C + I + G + (X − M)
C + S + T + M
C + I + G + (M − X)
C + I − G + (X − M)
questions.explain: AD equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, i.e. C + I + G + (X − M).

questions.q: The short-run Phillips curve illustrates a trade-off between:
options: Inflation and unemployment
Saving and investment
Economic growth and the balance of payments
Government spending and taxation
questions.explain: The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship (trade-off) between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment.

questions.q: If a government wishes to reduce a current account deficit using expenditure-reducing policy, it might:
options: Lower interest rates to encourage borrowing
Cut taxes to boost spending on imports
Use contractionary fiscal/monetary policy to reduce demand for imports
Increase government spending sharply
questions.explain: Reducing aggregate demand lowers demand for imports, helping to narrow a current account deficit, albeit at the cost of slower growth.

questions.q: Actual economic growth is best represented on a PPF diagram by:
options: An inward shift of the PPF
An outward shift of the PPF
A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the boundary
A movement along the PPF from one efficient point to another
questions.explain: Actual growth (using up spare capacity) is a movement from inside the frontier towards it, whereas an outward shift represents potential growth.

questions.q: A progressive tax system is one in which:
options: The average rate of tax falls as income rises
The average rate of tax rises as income rises
Only goods and services are taxed
Everyone pays the same percentage of income
questions.explain: Under a progressive tax the proportion of income paid in tax increases as income rises, helping to reduce inequality and act as an automatic stabiliser.

questions.q: Privatisation is a supply-side policy intended to improve efficiency because:
options: State ownership maximises profit
It guarantees lower prices in all cases
It removes the need for regulation
The profit motive and competition can increase productive and allocative efficiency
questions.explain: Transferring firms to the private sector is argued to sharpen incentives through the profit motive and competition, raising efficiency, though regulation may still be needed for natural monopolies.

questions.q: Which combination represents the components of aggregate demand most likely to fall during a recession driven by low confidence?
options: Imports and saving
Consumption and investment
Exports and the multiplier
Government spending and taxation
questions.explain: Falling confidence reduces consumer spending and firms' investment, the two most cyclically sensitive components of AD.

questions.q: The main aim of a central bank raising interest rates when the economy is overheating is to:
options: Raise the budget deficit
Increase aggregate demand
Reduce aggregate demand and inflationary pressure
Depreciate the exchange rate
questions.explain: Higher rates dampen borrowing and spending, reducing AD and easing demand-pull inflation when the economy is above capacity.

questions.q: Quantitative easing (QE) is best described as:
options: Increasing income tax to fund investment
The government cutting public spending to reduce the deficit
The central bank raising the base rate to curb inflation
The central bank creating money to buy assets, mainly government bonds, to increase the money supply
questions.explain: QE is an unconventional monetary policy in which the central bank purchases assets (chiefly government bonds) with newly created money to raise liquidity and lower yields.

questions.q: Real GDP is preferred to nominal GDP as a measure of growth because real GDP:
options: Counts only government output
Is always larger than nominal GDP
Includes the value of the black economy
Is adjusted for inflation/changes in the price level
questions.explain: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, allowing genuine changes in the volume of output to be measured.

questions.q: In the circular flow of income, which of the following is classified as an injection?
options: Imports
Taxation
Investment
Saving
questions.explain: Injections add to the circular flow and consist of investment, government spending and exports, whereas saving, taxation and imports are withdrawals.

questions.q: The 'multiplier effect' refers to the process by which:
options: The price level rises following an increase in costs
Higher interest rates reduce investment
Tax revenue rises automatically in a boom
A change in injections leads to a proportionately larger change in national income
questions.explain: An initial change in spending (an injection) generates further rounds of income and spending, producing a larger overall change in national income.

questions.q: Discretionary fiscal policy differs from automatic stabilisers because it involves:
options: Only the actions of the central bank
Deliberate, active changes to spending or taxation by the government
No change in government policy
Changes in the exchange rate
questions.explain: Discretionary fiscal policy involves deliberate decisions to alter spending or taxes, unlike automatic stabilisers which operate without new decisions.

questions.q: Which cost of inflation is described by money losing value so that savers and those on fixed incomes are worse off?
options: Menu costs
Shoe-leather costs
A fall in the real value of money and savings
Fiscal drag
questions.explain: Inflation erodes the real value of money and savings, redistributing income away from savers and people on fixed incomes towards borrowers.

questions.q: Contractionary monetary policy to reduce inflation would typically involve:
options: Raising the base rate to reduce borrowing and spending
Lowering the base rate and increasing QE
Increasing government spending
Cutting VAT
questions.explain: Raising interest rates increases the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, reducing AD and inflationary pressure.

questions.q: Supply-side policies aim primarily to:
options: Increase the productive capacity of the economy (shift LRAS right)
Increase the budget deficit
Reduce the exchange rate
Shift aggregate demand to the right
questions.explain: Supply-side policies seek to raise productivity and the quantity/quality of factors of production, shifting LRAS (and the PPF) outward.

questions.q: In the UK, monetary policy interest rate decisions are made by the:
options: Treasury
Financial Conduct Authority
Monetary Policy Committee of the Bank of England
Office for Budget Responsibility
questions.explain: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate to meet the government's inflation target.
